source.title: Learning from Failure: Training Debiased Classifier from Biased Classifier
source.authors: J. Nam; Hyuntak Cha; Sungsoo Ahn; Jaeho Lee; Jin-Woo Shin

page_placements.theme: Simple and spurious features link memorization to subgroup and shift failures

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses training-dynamics findings about noisy labels as motivation for its debiasing method, but does not test fitting randomly labeled data.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own results on biased datasets, including training dynamics for bias-aligned and bias-conflicting samples. It does not apply random labels, unstructured inputs, or the interventions named in V1–V5. Those biased-sample results are recorded under fits_no_version. The discussion of Arpit et al.'s noisy-label results is cited prior work, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: The study uses the easy-before-hard learning interpretation of Arpit et al. to motivate debiasing. Its own experiments compare bias-aligned and bias-conflicting samples with valid target labels; they do not compare real labels with noisy or random labels. Input corruptions retain object labels and do not test fitting unstructured inputs.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that LfF improves debiasing across synthetic and real-world datasets with minimal human supervision, using the observation that easier malignant bias attributes are learned earlier. Their approach assumes suitable bias and the availability of bias-conflicting training samples.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains paired networks with generalized cross entropy and relative-difficulty sample weighting on biased datasets; it does not use the random-label fitting setup in the cited sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that training dynamics differ between malignant and benign biases, and that performance varies with bias-aligned sample ratio and bias difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 2.3 and Figure 2 report that, under malignant bias, bias-aligned loss falls toward zero before bias-conflicting loss declines; under benign bias, the two loss trajectories are nearly indistinguishable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learning order for validly labeled samples depends on whether a spurious attribute is easier to learn than the target attribute.

fits_no_version.finding: Vanilla and GCE-biased models achieve 100% accuracy on bias-aligned samples; vanilla achieves about 50% on bias-conflicting samples, while the GCE-biased model is near chance. LfF achieves about 80% for both groups.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bias amplification and failure-based sample weighting change the balance of accuracy between bias-aligned and bias-conflicting samples.

record.peer_reviewed: 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020), as stated in the text
record.problems: The results relevant to training dynamics concern bias-aligned and bias-conflicting samples, not random labels. The described training-curve findings are reported in prose about Figure 4 without numerical uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for Table 2–10: those tables report evaluation accuracy for debiasing methods on biased datasets, not outcomes bearing on V1–V6. The paper's cited noisy-label findings are prior work, not this study's own results.

untested.parts: All: fitting completely random labels, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
All: relative training time for true and random labels and convergence across label-corruption fractions.
All: zero-error fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs. Gaussian-noise image corruption here does not constitute this experiment.
All: perfect training fit and steadily degrading test performance across random-label corruption fractions. Varying bias alignment is a different intervention.
All: necessity and sufficiency of explicit regularization for random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
All: learning shared real-label patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels. The noisy-label findings are attributed to prior work.

record.verdict_notes: No results warrant verdicts on V1–V6. The analogy between bias-conflicting samples and noisy-label samples does not make them measurements of the same claim.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting, chance test error, and whether the original architecture and training hyperparameters suffice.
Training time for true versus random labels and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across fractions of randomly corrupted labels.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
The paper does not compare learning real-label patterns with learning random or noisy labels; it examines bias-aligned and bias-conflicting samples instead.

relation.reason: The introduction and Section 2.3 connect the method to Arpit et al.'s noisy-label learning dynamics; the study does not itself compare learning real labels with learning noisy or random labels.

tranche.reason: LfF uses the easy-before-hard learning interpretation to motivate debiasing. Its experiments measure bias learning and debiasing with valid target labels, without testing any listed random-label version.

source_check.notes: The reported accuracies describe bias-aligned and bias-conflicting learning curves, not random-label memorization. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is consistent with the conclusion and the assumptions stated in Related Work.
